title: The Advice on How to Offer Praise Is Changing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article imports a shift in parenting advice about praise into the leadership context. The core distinction it examines is between authority-centered praise ('I'm proud of you') and person-centered praise ('You should be proud of what you did'), arguing that the former subtly makes the giver of praise the focal point and can create dependence on external validation, sometimes described as turning recipients into 'praise junkies.' The author extends this reasoning from parenting directly to leadership, arguing that leaders who habitually voice their own pride in a team member's work are unintentionally training that person to seek the leader's approval rather than developing internal confidence in their own judgment. The piece recommends a simple phrasing swap that redirects the focus of praise onto the achievement and the person who produced it.
points: The essay's central move is a precise phrasing distinction ('I'm proud of you' vs. 'you should be proud of what you did') rather than a general call to praise more or less.
It imports the concept of 'praise junkies' from parenting research directly into a workplace dependency dynamic between leaders and team members.
It reframes praise as a mechanism that can either build internal confidence or manufacture external validation-seeking, depending entirely on phrasing.
It offers specific reusable phrases ('You must be very pleased with what you accomplished') that leaders can adopt directly.
quotes: The argument that experts are making suggests that parents should never tell their children they are proud of them. At least not in the way everyone has traditionally been taught to.
I’m so proud of you” places the focus on the parent or leader. It robs children of the intrinsic motivation to learn from their work and the outcomes they produce.
Relying on external validation from an authority figure, experts reason, turns kids into “praise junkies.
In the workplace, leaders too often act “parentally” by doling out rewards and offering praise to those they deem deserving. This feels good but often creates a dependency.
Telling others they must be pleased, proud, or gratified about what they have accomplished places the focus exactly where it needs to be—on the quality of the work and the person who performed it.
